title: It didn’t start with rebellion.
paragraphs:
It didn’t start with rebellion.
It started with success.
And that’s why you didn’t notice it.

Because nothing looked broken.
Nothing felt sinful.
Nothing triggered alarm bells.

Prayer became optional.
Dependence became inconvenient.
God became… background noise.
How do you repent… of something the world is applauding?

You didn’t wake up one day and say,
“I don’t need God anymore.”

Stopped kneeling.
Stopped waiting.
Stopped trembling at His Word.
You just don’t need Him like before.

Not for decisions.
Not for provision.
Not for direction.

Because now you have systems.
Income.
Influence.
Because it doesn’t feel like sin.
But Scripture cuts through the illusion.

“You may say to yourself, ‘My power and the strength of my hands have produced this wealth for me.’
But remember the Lord your God, for it is He who gives you the ability to produce wealth…”

People who were blessed.
Provided for.
Established.
Pride doesn’t always look like arrogance.

No loud rebellion.
Just quiet independence.
In Revelation 3:17, Jesus speaks to a successful church:

“You say, ‘I am rich; I have acquired wealth and do not need a thing.’
But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind and naked.”
You can look strong… and be spiritually starving.

You can build an empire…
and lose intimacy.

You can win in public…
and drift in private.
The problem is not your success.
The problem is what success did to your heart.
But the Gospel says the opposite.

You were never enough.
That’s why Jesus came.
Sin is not just doing bad things.
And the call is not “do better.”
“Apart from Me, you can do nothing.”

Some scholars interpret this as not just inability in action,
but inability in eternal significance.
Because this is where everything changes.
You don’t have to earn your way back.
You don’t have to collapse everything you built.
You don’t have to punish yourself.
Because Jesus didn’t come for failures only.
He came for the self-sufficient too.

For the ones who stopped kneeling.
For the ones who outgrew their desperation.
For the ones who replaced dependence with control.
Jesus Christ carried not just your sins—

Your independence.
Your illusion of control.
And through His death and resurrection—

You sinned—even in your success.
You drifted—even while winning.
When was the last time you truly needed God?
Not because life is falling apart—
But because your heart is waking up.

Because the greatest miracle
is not success restored—
